patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Reyes is a 41-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman with obesity and chronic headaches who is admitted for evaluation of recurrent stereotyped paroxysmal episodes occurring for approximately 18 months. Episodes begin with a brief olfactory aura (burning rubber) followed by a rising epigastric sensation lasting 5-10 seconds, then loss of awareness with blank staring, lip-smacking, and rhythmic right-hand automatisms lasting 60-90 seconds, followed by 3-5 minutes of postictal confusion and mild expressive language difficulty. She has no memory of the events. Frequency was one per month initially but has increased to 3-4 per month over the past six months. On two occasions she has had focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures after sleep deprivation. She has not yet been told to stop driving but has self-restricted.

Ten months ago her primary care physician obtained a routine 1.5T brain MRI without contrast that was reported as 'no acute intracranial abnormality, normal study.' She was reassured and not referred to neurology. Her family physician subsequently attributed episodes to anxiety and panic disorder given chronic headaches and occasional palpitations; sertraline 50 mg was started one month ago but self-discontinued after two weeks due to nausea without symptomatic benefit.

Past history is notable for obesity, longstanding tension-type headaches (2-3 times per week over 5 years), and episodic left-ear pulsatile tinnitus attributed to eustachian tube dysfunction. No prior epilepsy diagnosis.

She was brought to neurology attention when a neurologist acquaintance witnessed one of her events at a community meeting and identified the semiology as stereotyped temporal lobe epilepsy. The consulting neurologist noted profound discordance between the clearly lateralizing left temporal EEG focus found on subsequent outpatient EEG and the normal routine MRI, and arranged urgent inpatient admission for dedicated epilepsy-protocol imaging and prolonged video-EEG monitoring. The diagnostic puzzle: the routine non-lesional MRI has anchored prior workup toward MRI-negative epilepsy or psychogenic etiology, while the progressive course, stereotyped mesial temporal semiology, and concordant left temporal EEG focus argue compellingly for a structural cause requiring dedicated skull-base imaging.

results.title: Temporal encephalocele as an under-recognized cause of drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy: prevalence, imaging characteristics, and surgical outcomes
results.summary: Temporal encephalocele (TE) is identified in 5-10% of patients referred for drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy evaluation. Lesions are typically located at the temporal pole and anteroinferior temporal region, herniating through defects in the floor of the middle cranial fossa. Standard MRI is insensitive to TE, particularly at 1.5T without thin-section skull-base sequences; dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI with 1 mm coronal sequences and CT bone windows substantially increases detection. Greater than 70% of patients achieve Engel class I-II outcomes following surgical repair.

results.title: Distinguishing temporal encephalocele-related epilepsy from mesial temporal sclerosis: semiology, EEG, and imaging patterns
results.journal: Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry
results.summary: Patients with temporal encephalocele present with seizures clinically indistinguishable from mesial temporal sclerosis (MTS): epigastric and olfactory auras, behavioral arrest, and oral automatisms are common to both. EEG shows anterior temporal interictal discharges and anterior temporal ictal onset in both syndromes. The key distinguishing feature is MRI: hippocampi are structurally normal in isolated TE, whereas MTS requires visible hippocampal signal change and volume loss on dedicated sequences. Dedicated thin-section MRI and CT skull base are required to avoid misclassification as MRI-negative TLE.

results.title: Association between temporal encephalocele, obesity, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension: pathophysiological mechanisms and clinical implications
results.summary: Obesity and idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) are recognized risk factors for acquired temporal encephalocele; elevated intracranial pressure may enlarge or unmask pre-existing small skull-base defects. Partial empty sella, pulsatile tinnitus, and papilledema may co-occur. Some patients with temporal encephalocele-related epilepsy have CSF opening pressures in the IIH range. Formal ophthalmologic evaluation and consideration of ICP measurement are warranted when these features co-occur with a temporal encephalocele.

results.title: ILAE evidence-based guideline: initial monotherapy and treatment of focal epilepsy
results.summary: For focal epilepsy, carbamazepine, levetiracetam, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, and lacosamide have Level A-B evidence as initial monotherapy. Drug-resistant epilepsy, defined as failure of two appropriate AEDs at adequate doses, should prompt re-evaluation for structural etiology and surgical candidacy.

output.summary: Temporal encephalocele is an under-recognized but surgically-remediable cause of drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy. Standard MRI frequently misses the diagnosis; dedicated epilepsy-protocol thin-section coronal MRI and CT skull base are required when routine MRI is non-lesional but EEG clearly lateralizes. Seizure semiology and EEG pattern mimic mesial TLE with hippocampal sclerosis; normal hippocampal volumes on dedicated sequences distinguish the two. An association with obesity and idiopathic intracranial hypertension has been reported. Evidence-based AED monotherapy (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, lacosamide) should be initiated while surgical evaluation proceeds.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Focal epilepsy of left temporal lobe origin (left temporal pole/anteroinferior temporal encephalocele through left middle cranial fossa floor defect)

differential.key_features: Routine 1.5T MRI read as normal anchors toward non-lesional TLE; dedicated epilepsy-protocol thin-section coronal imaging reveals the encephalocele and distinguishes the two.

differential.diagnosis: Temporal lobe epilepsy due to hippocampal sclerosis (mesial TLE/MTS)
differential.key_features: Clinically identical semiology (epigastric and olfactory aura, oral automatisms, contralateral hand automatisms) and anterior temporal EEG focus; distinguished by normal hippocampal volumes and signal on dedicated thin-section coronal MRI.
Prior attribution to anxiety/panic and normal routine MRI anchor toward PNES; video-EEG capturing habitual events with electrographic left temporal onset definitively excludes this.

Obesity, partial empty sella, pulsatile tinnitus, and blurred disc margins may distract toward IIH as the primary diagnosis; seizures in isolated IIH are not caused by elevated ICP and EEG does not lateralize to a structural epileptogenic focus in IIH alone.

Surgically remediable focal temporal lesion presenting with drug-resistant TLE is the same clinical scenario; excluded by MRI morphology showing cortical gray-matter protrusion through a bony defect rather than cortical expansion, T2-bright signal lesion, or contrast-enhancing mass.

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural cause (encephalocele vs. hippocampal sclerosis vs. truly non-lesional) should inform AED choice, as surgical candidacy affects the urgency and rationale for long-term medical therapy.

critical_actions: When routine MRI is non-lesional but EEG clearly lateralizes to a temporal focus, order dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI with 1 mm thin-section coronal sequences through the temporal poles and skull base — standard 1.5T axial brain MRI is insensitive to temporal pole and anteroinferior temporal abnormalities.

Recognize the left anteroinferior temporal encephalocele on dedicated MRI as the structural epileptogenic substrate concordant with the left temporal EEG focus; do not dismiss as artifactual or incidental.
Order CT skull base with bone windows to fully characterize the bony defect for surgical planning.
Initiate a non-enzyme-inducing AED (levetiracetam or lamotrigine preferred) while surgical evaluation is arranged.
Refer to a comprehensive epilepsy surgery center for evaluation of temporal encephalocele resection and skull-base repair given the drug-resistant course.
Counsel patient on driving restriction per local regulations and document seizure frequency and semiology.
contraindicated_actions: Do not conclude the evaluation as 'MRI-negative TLE' or 'idiopathic epilepsy' based solely on a standard 1.5T MRI without dedicated thin-section skull-base sequences.
Do not attribute the paroxysmal events to panic disorder or PNES on the basis of a normal routine MRI and prior anxiety history without video-EEG confirmation.

Do not use the incidental partial empty sella and borderline papilledema findings to attribute seizures to idiopathic intracranial hypertension without establishing the temporal encephalocele as the epileptogenic substrate on dedicated imaging.
key_reasoning_points: Temporal encephalocele through a middle cranial fossa floor defect is an under-recognized, surgically-remediable cause of drug-resistant TLE, reported in 5-10% of drug-resistant TLE surgical series; it is frequently missed on standard brain MRI.

Standard 1.5T axial brain MRI is inadequate for temporal pole and anteroinferior temporal region evaluation due to susceptibility artifact from the adjacent sphenoid bone — a dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI with 1 mm isotropic thin-section coronal sequences is required when routine MRI is non-lesional but EEG localizes.

Concordance across three modalities is the key to diagnosis: EEG (left anterior temporal interictal discharges and ictal F7/T3 onset), dedicated MRI (left temporal pole encephalocele at the concordant site), and FDG-PET (left anterior temporal hypometabolism) all localize to the same left temporal region.

Semiology is a critical localizing tool: olfactory and epigastric aura combined with right hand automatisms (contralateral to the left temporal focus) is the expected pattern for left temporal onset and must not be attributed to anxiety or panic.

The partial empty sella, pulsatile tinnitus, and blurred disc margins are associated features consistent with mildly elevated ICP in an obese patient (recognized IIH-encephalocele association) — important to identify but not the cause of the seizures.
Drug resistance after two appropriate AED trials should trigger re-evaluation for a structural epileptogenic substrate and surgical candidacy even when initial routine MRI was non-lesional.

red_herrings.data_point: Routine 1.5T brain MRI reported as 'no acute intracranial abnormality, normal study' — no epileptogenic lesion identified
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the diagnosis toward MRI-negative or idiopathic TLE, or toward PNES/panic disorder; may cause premature closure without dedicated epilepsy-protocol imaging.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Standard brain MRI is a known false-negative for temporal pole encephalocele due to susceptibility artifact from the sphenoid bone and absence of thin-section skull-base sequences; a non-lesional routine MRI does not exclude a structural epileptogenic substrate when EEG clearly lateralizes to a temporal focus.

red_herrings.data_point: Incidental partial empty sella with blurred optic disc margins, pulsatile tinnitus, and obesity
red_herrings.intended_effect: May distract toward idiopathic intracranial hypertension as the primary cause of all symptoms including the paroxysmal episodes, redirecting workup toward LP/ICP monitoring rather than epilepsy evaluation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Partial empty sella and signs of mildly elevated ICP are associated findings (the obesity-IIH-encephalocele association is recognized in the literature) but do not cause focal epileptic seizures; the primary epileptogenic substrate is the temporal encephalocele on dedicated imaging, concordant with the EEG focus.
